A table is a visualisation too. Column position, alignment, number
formatting, colour, weight: all visual properties, all mappings from data.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Useful functions

Part 3 uses one helper. It finds the limits of a colour scale from how the
values are spread. The exercises already define it, so you don't need to
copy it.

```{python}
import pandas as pd


def iqr_limits(values: pd.Series) -> list[float]:
    """
    Return colour scale limits centred on the median

    The limits are the same distance either side of the median, far enough
    to reach the farther outlier boundary. The boundaries lie 1.5
    interquartile ranges beyond the quartiles.

    Parameters
    ----------
    values
        The values to be coloured.

    Returns
    -------
    limits
        The lower and upper limit of the scale.
    """
    q1, median, q3 = values.quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
    step = 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
    low, high = q1 - step, q3 + step
    reach = max(median - low, high - median)
    return [median - reach, median + reach]
```
:::

## 3a. Tables deserve the same care as plots

Here are the provisional census figures again, as a plain DataFrame: one
row per tribe, with its population in 2014 and in 2024.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_0
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT

def load(version):
    p2014 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2014.csv")
    p2024 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2024.csv")
    return p2014.merge(p2024, on="tribe", suffixes=("_2014", "_2024"))

provisional = load("bad")
provisional
```

And here is the same data as a finished table:

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT, html

def load(version):
    p2014 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2014.csv")
    p2024 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2024.csv")
    return p2014.merge(p2024, on="tribe", suffixes=("_2014", "_2024"))

provisional = load("bad")
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .tab_source_note(
        "Source: UBOS, National Population and Housing Census 2024, provisional results"
    )
)
```

The finished table is easier to read: it has a title, the numbers have
thousands separators, and the tribe names are set apart from the data.

But it hides the error just as well as the UBOS table did. Better-looking
isn't enough. To reveal the error, a table needs a better **mapping**:
it has to show the right values, in a way the eye can compare. We'll build
up to that in 3d, where you add the missing column yourself.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [tables_1, tables_2, tables_3, tables_4, growth_1]
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT

def load(version):
    p2014 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2014.csv")
    p2024 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2024.csv")
    return p2014.merge(p2024, on="tribe", suffixes=("_2014", "_2024"))

provisional = load("bad")
```

The exercises from 3d onwards start with the `growth` column already added:

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [format_1, format_2, rebuild_1]
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT

def load(version):
    p2014 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2014.csv")
    p2024 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2024.csv")
    df = p2014.merge(p2024, on="tribe", suffixes=("_2014", "_2024"))
    df["growth"] = df.population_2024 / df.population_2014 - 1
    return df

provisional = load("bad")
corrected = load("good")

def iqr_limits(values: pd.Series) -> list[float]:
    """
    Return colour scale limits centred on the median

    The limits are the same distance either side of the median, far enough
    to reach the farther outlier boundary. The boundaries lie 1.5
    interquartile ranges beyond the quartiles.

    Parameters
    ----------
    values
        The values to be coloured.

    Returns
    -------
    limits
        The lower and upper limit of the scale.
    """
    q1, median, q3 = values.quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
    step = 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
    low, high = q1 - step, q3 + step
    reach = max(median - low, high - median)
    return [median - reach, median + reach]
```

## 3b. Building a table step by step

A great-tables table starts with `GT()`: pass it the data. Each method
you chain on adds one piece of structure, just as each `+` adds a layer in
plotnine.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_1
GT(provisional)
```

Tell `GT()` which column holds the row labels:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_2
GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
```

`rowname_col="tribe"` moves the tribe names out of the data and into the
**stub**, the column of row labels on the left.

Add a title and subtitle with `tab_header()`:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_3
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title=___, subtitle=___)
)
```

::: {.hint exercise="tables_3"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Titles are text, so put them in quotes: `title="Population by tribe"`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="tables_3"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_3
#| solution: true
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
)
```
:::
:::

Now group the two population columns under one heading with
`tab_spanner()`, give the columns short labels with `cols_label()`, and
credit the source with `tab_source_note()`:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_4
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=[___, ___])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024")
    .tab_source_note(
        "Source: UBOS, National Population and Housing Census 2024, provisional results"
    )
)
```

::: {.hint exercise="tables_4"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`columns` takes a list of column names from the data, in quotes.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="tables_4"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_4
#| solution: true
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024")
    .tab_source_note(
        "Source: UBOS, National Population and Housing Census 2024, provisional results"
    )
)
```
:::
:::

A spanner groups *columns* the way `facet_wrap()` groups plots: it shows
which values belong together.

## 3c. Which component?

Match each letter to a part of the table: **header**, **column label**,
**stub**, **body**, **footer**, **spanner**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
def tag(letter):
    return (
        '<span style="display:inline-block;width:16px;height:16px;'
        "line-height:16px;font-size:11px;text-align:center;border-radius:50%;"
        "background:#d7301f;color:white;font-weight:bold;"
        f'vertical-align:super;margin-left:3px">{letter}</span>'
    )

labelled = load("good").head(3)[["tribe", "population_2014", "population_2024"]]
for col in ["population_2014", "population_2024"]:
    labelled[col] = labelled[col].map("{:,}".format)
labelled.loc[1, "tribe"] = labelled.loc[1, "tribe"] + tag("B")
labelled.loc[2, "population_2024"] = tag("D") + labelled.loc[2, "population_2024"]

(
    GT(labelled, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title=html("Population by tribe" + tag("C")))
    .tab_spanner(
        label=html("Population" + tag("F")),
        columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"]
    )
    .cols_label(population_2014=html("2014" + tag("A")), population_2024="2024")
    .fmt_markdown(columns=["tribe", "population_2024"])
    .cols_align("right", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .tab_source_note(html("Source: UBOS, 2024 census" + tag("E")))
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Letter | Component    | Made with           |
|--------|--------------|---------------------|
| A      | column label | `cols_label()`      |
| B      | stub         | `rowname_col=`      |
| C      | header       | `tab_header()`      |
| D      | body         | the data            |
| E      | footer       | `tab_source_note()` |
| F      | spanner      | `tab_spanner()`     |
:::

## 3d. Formatting as mapping

The error is in the *change* between 2014 and 2024, and no column shows
that. Choosing to show it is a mapping decision, and it is yours to make.
Add a `growth` column: the 2024 population divided by the 2014 population,
minus 1. A value of 0.25 means the tribe grew by 25%.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: growth_1
provisional["growth"] = provisional.population_2024 / provisional.___ - 1
provisional
```

::: {.hint exercise="growth_1"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Growth compares the new population with the old one. Which column holds
the old one?
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="growth_1"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: growth_1
#| solution: true
provisional["growth"] = provisional.population_2024 / provisional.population_2014 - 1
provisional
```
:::
:::

The exercises below add this column for you, so each one stands alone.

The table now shows raw values: `5555412` and `0.27`. The `fmt_*()` methods
map those values to readable text. Format the population columns as whole
numbers and the growth column as a percentage:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: format_1
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024", growth="Growth")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .fmt_percent(columns="growth", decimals=0)
)
```

Every number is now readable, and the error is *in* the table: in ten
years, Bagisu shrank by 12% and Acholi by 9%, while every other tribe grew.
Bakiga doubled. But you still have to read each row to find it.

Colour can do that work. `data_color()` maps each value to a background
colour. First we need to decide which values get which colours.
`iqr_limits()`, defined at the top of this page, sets the scale from how
the tribes' growth is spread. Pass its result to `data_color()` as the
`domain`:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: format_2
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024", growth="Growth")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .fmt_percent(columns="growth", decimals=0)
    .data_color(
        columns="growth",
        palette=["#c13d31", "white", "#1570d1"],
        domain=iqr_limits(provisional.growth),
        truncate=True,
    )
)
```

The same table that hid the error now shows it at a glance. Nothing about
the data changed; we chose a different mapping.

::: {.callout-important}
## Why these colours?

`palette` lists three colours, and `domain` gives the range of values
they span. `iqr_limits()` puts white halfway, at the median growth (31%),
and the red and blue ends at the same distance either side. That distance
reaches the usual boundary for an outlier: 1.5 interquartile ranges beyond
the quartiles. Values beyond that boundary take the end colour,
because of `truncate=True`.

The quartiles come from the middle half of the tribes, so a few wrong
values barely move the scale. Normal growth fades to white, and anything
*unusual* stands out, in either direction: too slow (red) or too fast
(blue).

Try centring the scale on zero instead: `domain=[-1, 1]`. Which errors can
you still see?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Bakiga still stands out in dark blue. But every other growing tribe turns
blue too, and **Bagisu and Acholi fade to a pale pink**: −12% is a small
step from zero on a scale that runs to ±100%. The most impossible numbers
in the table, populations *shrinking*, become the hardest to see.

Where the scale is centred is a design choice, and it decides what the
reader notices. (Without `truncate=True`, values outside `domain` are
coloured grey.)
:::

## 3e. Build the corrected table

Now build a table for the corrected figures yourself, from `GT()` up. The
`corrected` DataFrame is ready, with the `growth` column. Aim for a table
where an error would have been obvious *before* publication. Include:

- the tribes as row labels
- a title and subtitle
- a "Population" spanner over the two years
- readable population and growth figures
- colour on the growth column, as in 3d
- the source

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: rebuild_1
(
    GT(corrected, rowname_col="tribe")
    # your code here
)
```

::: {.solution exercise="rebuild_1"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: rebuild_1
#| solution: true
(
    GT(corrected, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024", growth="Growth")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .fmt_percent(columns="growth", decimals=0)
    .data_color(
        columns="growth",
        palette=["#c13d31", "white", "#1570d1"],
        domain=iqr_limits(corrected.growth),
        truncate=True
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        "Source: UBOS, National Population and Housing Census 2024, corrected results"
    )
)
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## What do you see?

How does this table look, compared with the provisional one in 3d?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

The four tribes that were solid red or blue are now close to white. In
the corrected table only **Lugbara** is an outlier, and it stays red. Its
growth is low (12% over the ten years) next to a typical 27%.

The colour tells you what is *unusual*. It does not tell you whether
something is *wrong*. An outlier is a prompt to stop and think. Check the
figures and how they were produced. Only then can you say whether it is an
error or a real difference.

Some other cells still carry a pale tint. The tribes in the corrected table
grew at very similar rates, so its scale is narrow, and a small difference
from the median shows as colour. Each table has its own scale, so only
compare colours within one table.
:::

## Plot or table?

In 2f, a plot revealed the error: the change was mapped to the length and
direction of a line. Here a table revealed it: the change was mapped to a
number *and* a colour.

The plot is quicker for spotting a pattern. The table keeps the exact
values, which is what a census report must publish. Both work for the same
reason: they map the growth, not only the raw counts.
